891.quote_or_event: “He should never do anything disagreeable to the wise, neither in words nor deeds, neither openly nor secretly.”
891.explanation: Mahāvīra's first lecture on discipline (vinaya) makes giving no offence to the wise, in word, deed, public or private, a basic rule for anyone who wishes to prosper.
891.tie_back: The Kural makes not belittling the great the first of all self-protections, and the Uttarādhyayana likewise puts care never to offend the wise at the foundation of right conduct.
891.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 1.17 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
891._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close in spirit; the Jain rule is framed as monastic discipline toward teachers rather than as worldly self-protection.

892.quote_or_event: “O lord of the fair hill-land resounding with streams! we should not, thinking they will forgive us, do what is hateful to the guiltless, for none can remove their anger when once they are provoked.”
892.explanation: The first quatrain of the Nāladiyār's chapter 'Against reproaching the great' warns against wronging the worthy on the assumption that they will forgive, because their anger once roused cannot be undone.
892.tie_back: The Kural says disregard for the great brings affliction that will not leave, and the Jain Tamil quatrain names the same lasting, irremovable consequence.
892.source: Nāladiyār 17.1 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
892._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib.org. Tamil Jain literature whose chapter title matches the Kural's adhikaram; the 'irremovable' consequence is close, though the quatrain speaks of the guiltless rather than the powerful.

893.quote_or_event: “Like a poisonous snake is a great sage of severe austerities, of tremendous piety and power; like a swarm of moths you will rush into a fire, if you beat a monk on his begging tour.”
893.explanation: When brahmin youths beat the outcaste-born monk Harikeśa, Bhadrā warns them that assaulting such a sage is like moths rushing into a flame, a ruin they bring on themselves.
893.tie_back: The Kural says that whoever wants to be ruined need only offend those able to destroy, and Bhadrā's image of moths flying into the fire is that same self-chosen destruction.
893.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
893._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit; in the Jain story the sage himself feels no hatred (12.32) and the punishment comes from his attendant Yakṣas, which softens the parallel.

894.quote_or_event: “You may as well dig rocks with your nails, or eat iron with your teeth, or kick fire with your feet, as treat contemptuously a monk.”
894.explanation: Bhadrā lists three absurd, self-wounding acts to show how futile and harmful it is for ordinary people to scorn a monk of great spiritual power.
894.tie_back: The Kural says that when the powerless harm the powerful they are beckoning Death with their own hand, and Bhadrā's picture of kicking fire is the same harm turned back on oneself.
894.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.26 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
894._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Very close in structure (the weak harming the strong is self-destruction); the 'great' here are ascetics of spiritual power, not worldly rulers.

895.quote_or_event: “Like as the golden-coloured serpent trembles, though in Patala, if he hear the sound of the fierce anger of the thunder in the heavens, so enemies, though they have shut themselves up in a fort difficult of access, will not be able to escape when the great are angry.”
895.explanation: In the Nāladiyār's chapter against reproaching the great, a serpent deep in the underworld still trembles at thunder, and so enemies cannot hide even in a strong fort once the great are angry.
895.tie_back: The Kural says those who incur a mighty king's anger will not survive wherever they flee, and the quatrain makes the same point that no refuge holds when the great are roused.
895.source: Nāladiyār 17.4 (English translation serialised in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
895._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against the Indian Antiquary translation on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one on the impossibility of escape; this is Tamil Jain didactic poetry rather than canonical scripture, and it speaks of 'the great' rather than specifically a king.

896.quote_or_event: “He is the man of great fame and might, of awful piety and power; do not injure him who cannot be injured, lest he consume you all by the fire (of his virtue).”
896.explanation: Bhadrā tells the youths attacking Harikeśa that a sage of such power cannot truly be harmed, and that wronging him risks being consumed by the fire of his virtue.
896.tie_back: The Kural says a man burnt by fire may survive but those who offend the great will not escape, and the Jain verse pictures offending a sage as calling down a fire that would consume them all.
896.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
896._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Shares the fire imagery and the danger of offending the great, but lacks the Kural's comparison in which ordinary fire is the lesser peril.

897.quote_or_event: “Prostrate yourself before him for protection, you together with all of them, if you want to save your life and your property; for in his wrath he might reduce the world to ashes.”
897.explanation: Bhadrā urges the priest and his household to seek the offended monk's forgiveness at once, since life and property alike are forfeit if such a sage is roused.
897.tie_back: The Kural asks what good a splendid life and great wealth are once the truly worthy turn their anger on someone, and the Jain verse puts life and property at stake before an offended sage in the same way.
897.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 12.28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
897._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good fit on life and wealth being worthless against the anger of the worthy; Jain ethics nonetheless holds that the true sage does not act from wrath, as Harikeśa himself says (12.32).

898.quote_or_event: Kṛṣṇa, learning that his drunken sons and nephews had beaten the meditating ascetic Dvaipāyana almost to death, thought: “Oh! this lack of restraint on the part of these princes will be the death of the family.” Dvaipāyana, reborn as a fire-deity, later burned Dvārakā with its people.
898.explanation: In Hemacandra's Neminātha-caritra the Yādava clan, which seemed securely established, perishes with its city because its princes assaulted an ascetic.
898.tie_back: The Kural warns that when those great as mountains are slighted, even people who seemed permanently established perish with their families, and the destruction of the Yādavas and Dvārakā is that fate told in full.
898.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 8 (Neminātha-caritra), ch. 11, part 2 'Beating of Dvaipāyana' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
898._accuracy_note: Kṛṣṇa's words are checked word for word against Johnson's translation on wisdomlib.org; the surrounding narrative is paraphrased. Very close in plot, but Jain tradition condemns Dvaipāyana's anger and his vow of revenge (nidāna) rather than holding it up as just.

899.quote_or_event: “Enough of this conciliatory talk of yours, Kṛṣṇa. Beaten by your sons, I have made a nidāna—to burn Dvārakā with its people. There is no escape from that, except of you.”
899.explanation: When Kṛṣṇa, king of Dvārakā, begs the injured ascetic for pardon, Dvaipāyana refuses and vows to burn the royal city, and Kṛṣṇa loses his capital and kingdom.
899.tie_back: The Kural says that when those who hold high vows flare up in anger even a king is broken midway and loses his kingdom, and Kṛṣṇa, unable to appease an angered ascetic, sees his city destroyed.
899.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 8 (Neminātha-caritra), ch. 11, part 2 (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
899._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Johnson on wisdomlib.org. The plot fits closely, but Jainism treats Dvaipāyana's nidāna as a spiritual failure, and Kṛṣṇa's own words in the same passage call anger a great enemy, so the Jain lesson differs from the Kural's.

900.quote_or_event: “What is this delusion of yours? You were told earlier, indeed, that there was no escape for any one here, except you two.”
900.explanation: As Dvārakā burns, Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, the mightiest heroes of their age, haul their parents' chariot to the gate by their own strength, but the fire-god Dvaipāyana tells them no one else can be saved.
900.tie_back: The Kural says that even those with boundless support and powerful allies cannot escape once the truly great are angered, and the Yādavas, protected by Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma themselves, still perish.
900.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 8 (Neminātha-caritra), ch. 11, part 2 (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
900._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Johnson on wisdomlib.org. Strong narrative fit for 'support does not save'; this is the third use of the Dvaipāyana episode in this chapter, and the Jain text frames the outcome as karma and fate as well as the ascetic's anger.
